Minor: bench.py:7 imports the sibling eda-proposers by sys.path insertion while pyproject.toml declares dependencies = []; bench.py:14-20 caches the true HV by id(space), which can go stale if a Space is freed and its id reused; halton() silently stops at i=20000 and appends the rest lexicographically; latin() uses unnormalised index L1 while the farthest order uses range-normalised L1; run.py writes with an unclosed open().write.
evidence.claims: Backed by results.txt and my recomputation: the whole results table, +0.014/+0.042 at b8, 'within 0.002' at b40, Halton stalling to 75, ranks 0.98/0.99, median 90% budgets 7/15/15/15/17, '+0.01 to +0.04 from 8 to 20'. Not backed or overstated: (1) README.md:10 headline 'a space-filling order (Halton ...) reaches 90% ... in 7 to 15 evaluations': Halton's 7 and 0.926 at b8 are the best of 48 equally valid Halton labellings (6 axis-to-base assignments x 8 level reversals), whose b8 mean is 0.854 (median 0.859, min 0.746); the README does caveat 'single draws' at :44 and says relabelled axes 'would be needed' at :48, but that test is free on this table and was not run. (2) README.md:17 'batches of 8 designs that each use every level of every axis about once': only the first batch is guaranteed; in 318 of 500 batches (50 seeds) the 8 p levels are not distinct. (3) README.md:41 'worse than all 300 random orders at every budget to 30': 299 of 300 at b16. AI-assistance line, 'stylised and preliminary' and limitations are present and honest.
evidence.fitness: A researcher maintaining eda-harness can act on the core finding (lexicographic is a bad default; any space-filling order or a shuffle is better) and the code is reusable. But it is not a research contribution: that space-filling designs beat a lexicographic sweep at small budgets is textbook DoE, and none of the prior work is cited (grep for McKay, Latin hypercube, Johnson, Morris, maximin literature, scrambled/randomised QMC: none in README.md). One 80-design table with a 12-point front that is a sub-grid; the ranking among space-filling orders is, as the README admits, not established.
evidence.domain: Against standard DoE practice: the Halton implementation is correct (bases 2,3,5, index from 1, snapped to the grid; verified independently), and the greedy maximin is a standard farthest-point traversal on range-normalised L1. Departures: a deterministic QMC point set is normally randomised (Cranley-Patterson shift, Owen scrambling, or at least the arbitrary axis/base assignment averaged) before its performance is compared with random sampling; doing that here (my 48 relabellings) cuts Halton's b8 lead over random from +0.118 to about +0.046 on average, with 42/48 still above the random mean. 'latin' is a greedy nearest-match heuristic, not a Latin hypercube after the first batch. Comparisons use unpaired intervals of the mean over 300 seeds, adequate here given the gaps.

defects.what: Headline credits Halton with 90% of the front in 7 evaluations and 0.926 at budget 8, but that is the best of 48 equally valid Halton labellings of this grid (axis-to-base assignment x level direction); their mean at b8 is 0.854 (median 0.859, min 0.746) against random 0.808. The README caveats 'single draws' (:44) and says relabelled axes 'would be needed' (:48), but the test is free on this table and was not run, so the headline overstates what Halton buys.

Tests do not constrain the core: 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive (Halton base assignment, maximin distance update min->max, bootstrap percentiles 2.5/97.5 -> 25/75, Latin target permutation); no test pins a number in results.txt.

No prior work on space-filling designs is cited and novelty is not stated: Latin hypercube (McKay, Beckman & Conover 1979), Halton (1960), maximin distance designs (Johnson, Moore & Ylvisaker 1990; Morris & Mitchell 1995), randomised QMC. That space-filling beats a lexicographic sweep at small budgets is textbook DoE; the project should say it is confirming this for the harness default.

'latin' is described as batches that each use every level of every axis about once; only the first batch is exact (greedy nearest-match fallback), and 318 of 500 batches over 50 seeds repeat a p level.
'worse than all 300 random orders at every budget to 30' is false at budget 16: one random order scores below lexicographic (1/300, rounded to 0.00 in results.txt).
pyproject description promises a 'stride' order that is not implemented.
Imports the sibling eda-proposers via sys.path insertion while pyproject declares dependencies = []; true HV cached by id(space).

verdict: The numbers are right: an independent exact-fraction recomputation (own Halton, own maximin, own hypervolume by two methods) reproduces every deterministic cell of results.txt, my own random shuffles and a normal-approximation check reproduce the stochastic means and intervals, and run.py and figure.py regenerate the committed files byte-identically. The finding that lexicographic order is a poor harness default is sound. It falls short of the bar on claims and verification: the headline Halton result is the best of 48 equivalent labellings (mean 0.854 at budget 8, not 0.926), 'latin' is not Latin after the first batch, two smaller claims round past the data, 4 of 5 seeded core mutants survive, and the space-filling-design literature that makes the result expected is not cited. A useful engineering note for eda-harness, not yet a research result.
